Player B has no chance to get any Victory Point and
makes a deal with player E. The terms of the deal
are that player B will help player E oust E's prey,
if player E helps B on ousting B's prey (after which,
player B would commit suicide).

Later in the game, B grows stronger and has
real chances to win the game.

Is player B forced to break his or her deal with
player E, because he must play to win (and he now
has real chances to do so)?

Greetings,
Damnans

> If you can convince the judge that doing so doesn't reduce your

The play-to-win rule has about as much teeth as the average UN Resolution
(whoo! hooo! asbestos underwear: ON!). It's great as a general reminder
of what should be the proper spirit of the game, but would-be judges
looking to it to help decide when to put someone else's game on remote
control are wasting their time. Any deck, any deck at all, could have a
single copy of Dramatic Upheaval. Any player could claim to be throwing a
game, only to break whatever seppeku deal he acted like he was making
and knife his way into a VP in fantastic Jyhad style. Only after the
fact, after the game is over, can you look back and decide whether someone
was playing to win or not, if even then. It will be too late to affect
the game in question, but you could always warn/admonish/decapitate the
player anyway, and that may affect future games.

This "ANYONE can do ANYTHING and it can happen at ANY TIME" attitude is
called the "Josh Duffin Defense", and is most often used to remove
nearly all deal-making within the game structure. I haven't seen it
used in this way, however, and it is quite interesting!

"Any deck, any deck at all, could have a single copy of Dramatic
Upheaval."

Point: As a judge, you have the ability to stop the game to look through
every card in every deck, if necessary. So do it. I've done this
*twice* at Origins, each time because a deal hinged on it.

"Any player could claim to be throwing a game, only to break whatever
seppeku deal he acted like he was making and knife his way into a VP in
fantastic Jyhad style."

Point: As a judge, you have the ability to stop the game to take the
"crazy Malkavian" player aside and ask him what the hell he is doing.
So do it. At Origins last year, I was *forced* to stop the finals of a
tournament to take a player aside who, between what he was saying and
what was in his hand and in play, had utterly confused me (as the
judge). I took him 50 feet away from the play area, he gave me a
15-second explanation which had to do somewhat with his BSing ability
(which I will not relate here), and I was *completely* convinced of what
was happening.

"Only after the fact, after the game is over, can you look back and
decide whether someone was playing to win or not, if even then."

Point: If you have to wait until the game is over to become unconfused,
or to settle whatever issue(s) you have with what is happening within
the game structure, you haven't fully done your job as the judge. *When
it becomes necessary*, don't be afraid to take an active role in the
game!

No. The player is specifically allowed to honor a legally-made
deal even if the "must play to win" rule would oblige the player to
take some other course of action in the absence of the deal. This
means that his action (honoring the deal, when breaking the deal
would increase his VPs) is outside the scope of the deal-blind
rules. It is still legal to honor a legally-made deal.

Yeah, and what you say is "it's his game, you can't say he isn't playing
to win until he's lost." There are lots of clear rules that the judge can
consult and execute based upon an observable, present state. The "play to
win" rule isn't one of them. You can't make a ruling on it because:

A) Playing to win is an *intention*. You have no way to ascertain what
someone's intention is except by their testimony. The problem of
testimony is a well-known conundrum in the philosophy of knowledge.

state. To really drive it home, that future state requires that the game
be over (or maybe that someone's gotten three VP's, if you want to get
picky). You can not determine if this future state will follow
deterministically from the present state. The closing paragraph of
Wittgenstein's Tractatus sums it up nicely: "Of that which you do not
know, you must remain silent"[1].

There are several cases where I can see someone not playing to win. In no
particular order -

Collusion (or the equivalent): Obviously undesirable. Your proposal would
have minimal effect as the colluders would just focus on manipulating TWs to
the exclusion of everything else.

Putting the tournament before the games: I don't have any problem with this.
But, if you really want to encourage people to focus on each individual game,
dole out prizes based on TWs rather than making the finals. Or, play single
round tournaments. No? Then maybe playing to each game instead of the
tournament isn't that important?

Spite/despair/etc.: This is annoying, but I don't see it having a lot of
effect. Sure, within a given tournament, the throwing of a game can be
important. But, it tends to be random in who it hurts (much like, say, seating
order) and over time, the better players will do better than the worse players.

Random game element: Also annoying but where anyone can be frustrated to the
point of giving up on a game (previous category), random game elements should
be kept away from tournaments. Can probably do this by putting a heftier price
on playing in the tournament effectively forcing them to pay everyone else for
their selfish desires since they won't be as likely to score prizes. Whatever
scoring system you have in place isn't going to mean anything to these people.

Besides competing and trying to score prizes, I can't think of a reason to play
in tournaments. The people into competing should be playing to win because,
uh, that's what competing means. The people trying to score prizes, their
behavior can be manipulated by the prize distribution scheme. Rules against
cheating (which I don't think not playing to win falls under) cover, uh,
cheating.
